_readme: The 36 principles: for each number, the Step, Tradition and Concept with the thread that connects them. Drives /principles/, the twelve /principles/N/ pages, the meeting focus and the printable handouts. The 'text' fields are EMPTY on purpose: paste the official short-form wording from your own A.A. literature (Big Book pp. 59–60 and Appendix I; The A.A. Service Manual) if the committee decides to show it; until then the site links each number to aa.org.
notice: The Twelve Steps, Twelve Traditions and Twelve Concepts for World Service are copyrighted by Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, Inc. Read them in full at aa.org.
principleWordsNote: The principle words below are the ones members commonly cite in Step, Tradition and Concept study; they are a study aid passed along in meetings, not A.A. literature, and other lists exist.

concept.label: The Twelve Concepts for World Service at aa.org

step.gist: Admitting powerlessness over alcohol and an unmanageable life

tradition.gist: The group's welfare first, because no one recovers alone

concept.gist: The whole Fellowship holds final say over world services

thread.title: Where the power lives
thread.oneLiner: Admitting I have none, I discover where real power lives: in the group, and in the whole Fellowship's conscience.
thread.summary: Step One begins with an admission that I cannot run my own life. Tradition One says the group comes before any one of us, because without the group no one gets sober. Concept I places final authority for A.A.'s world services in the whole Fellowship rather than in any office or board. All three answer the same question, not who is in charge but where the power actually lives, and the answer each time is: not in me alone.
thread.weave: A newcomer who has finally admitted that willpower failed is already living Concept I without knowing it; the power to recover turned out to be outside himself, in a roomful of people who had been where he was. A home group practices the same thing when a member who wants the meeting run her way sets that aside because the group's welfare matters more than her preference. At the district and area level, the GSR carries her group's conscience rather than merely her own opinion, and the delegate carries the area's conscience to the Conference while remembering that, once there, he serves A.A. as a whole. Even the trustees and the staff at GSO serve at the pleasure of the groups, who hold the ultimate say through the Conference. The thread runs unbroken from one surrendered drunk to a Fellowship of some two million members: the power was never ours to hold alone.
questions: Where did I first notice that the power to stay sober was not mine alone?
When has my home group put its common welfare ahead of a strong personality, and what happened?
If the groups hold final authority, how does my group actually exercise it between Conferences?

step.gist: Coming to believe a greater Power can restore us

tradition.gist: God speaks through the group conscience; leaders serve, never rule

concept.gist: The groups entrust the Conference to speak and act for them

thread.title: How God speaks to us
thread.oneLiner: A Power greater than ourselves speaks through a group conscience, and the Conference is that conscience for the whole Fellowship.
thread.summary: Step Two asks us to believe that something greater than ourselves can restore us. Tradition Two tells us where that Power is found for the group: in the collective conscience, with leaders who serve rather than govern. Concept II extends the idea worldwide: the groups have handed the Conference the job of speaking and acting as the conscience of A.A. in its world affairs. In each case the same Power speaks, through one heart, through one group, through a body of delegates.
thread.weave: Most of us came to believe not through a thunderbolt but by watching sober people stay sober, and that quiet evidence was our first group conscience. In a home group business meeting, a loving God shows up in the discussion itself; the chairperson keeps the floor fair and lets the group, not the chair, decide. When a GSR reports back and the group adjusts its thinking, the two-way flow Bill W. hoped for is working. At the Conference each spring, delegates from every area in the U.S. and Canada gather with the trustees, directors and staff for a week, pray, discuss and vote, and the Fellowship trusts that what emerges is as close to God's will for A.A. as we are likely to get. Hope at the kitchen table and hope in the Conference room are the same hope.
questions: What first gave me hope that a Power greater than myself could do what I could not?
How does my home group make room for that Power to speak at a business meeting?
What would change if I trusted the Conference's conscience the way I trust my group's?

step.gist: Choosing to let a Higher Power direct our lives

tradition.gist: Wanting to stop drinking is all it takes to belong

concept.gist: Trusted servants may use their own judgment within their role

thread.title: The decision to trust
thread.oneLiner: Trusting God with my will, trusting a stranger's desire to stop drinking, trusting a servant's judgment: all one act of faith.
thread.summary: Step Three is a decision to stop running the show and let God's care direct our lives. Tradition Three makes the same leap on behalf of the group: we trust that anyone with a desire to stop drinking belongs, no credentials required. Concept III asks the Fellowship to trust its servants with a Right of Decision, letting them use judgment rather than binding them with instructions on every point. Each is a decision to let go of control and extend trust.
thread.weave: An alcoholic making the Third Step decision is admitting that running every detail herself was the problem, not the solution. A home group lives the same decision when it stops asking whether a newcomer is really an alcoholic, or sober enough, or the right sort of person, and simply says welcome. When a group sends its GSR to an area assembly, Tradition Three's trust becomes Concept III's Right of Decision: the GSR hears the discussion, learns something the group did not know, and votes her conscience rather than a rigid instruction carried from home. Delegates at the Conference do the same, and the trustees in turn are trusted to act on Conference advice without a committee hovering over every detail. Faith in God, faith in the newcomer and faith in our trusted servants are three expressions of the same willingness to let go.
questions: What am I still trying to control that Step Three invites me to release?
Has my group ever added an unwritten requirement for membership, and how did it affect newcomers?
When I send my GSR to an assembly, do I give instructions or do I give trust?

step.gist: Taking an honest, searching look at ourselves

tradition.gist: Each group runs its own affairs, mindful of others

concept.gist: Everyone who serves gets a vote in proportion to responsibility

thread.title: Owning our own affairs
thread.oneLiner: Courage to take stock of my own life, freedom for a group to run its own, and a real vote for everyone who serves.
thread.summary: Step Four takes courage because it asks us to look squarely at our own part in things, without blaming anyone else. Tradition Four gives each group the freedom, and the responsibility, to manage its own affairs, as long as it does not harm other groups or A.A. as a whole. Concept IV guarantees that everyone who carries service responsibility also gets a voice and a vote, in proportion to that responsibility. The thread is ownership: no one else can take my inventory, run my group or cast my vote for me.
thread.weave: The member writing a Fourth Step learns that resentments usually point back to her own fears and choices, and that facing them is both frightening and freeing. A home group exercising Tradition Four decides its own format, its own literature table and its own Seventh Tradition split, and takes a periodic group inventory to ask honestly how well it is carrying the message. That same group also pauses before a decision that might affect the groups next door, because autonomy ends where harm to others begins. At the area assembly, Concept IV means the GSR from a group of six has a vote alongside the DCM and the area officers, and at the Conference the trustees, directors and GSO and Grapevine staff vote alongside the delegates rather than merely advising them. Courage to look, freedom to act and a seat at the table belong together.
questions: What fear keeps me from looking at my own part in a resentment?
When did my group last take an inventory of itself, and what did it find?
Who in my district or area carries real responsibility without a vote, and why?

step.gist: Sharing our inventory out loud with God and another person

tradition.gist: One purpose: carrying the message to the suffering alcoholic

concept.gist: Minority voices are heard; grievances get a fair hearing

thread.title: Speaking the hard truth
thread.oneLiner: Step Five says it out loud, Tradition Five keeps the message plain, and Concept V makes sure the quiet voice gets heard.
thread.summary: Step Five is where private honesty becomes spoken honesty: we tell another human being the exact nature of what we found. Tradition Five keeps the group honest about what it is for, carrying one message to one kind of sufferer rather than drifting into everything else. Concept V protects the honesty of the whole structure by guaranteeing that a minority view is heard and a grievance can be appealed, so that an uncomfortable truth is never simply outvoted into silence. Integrity, in all three, means the whole truth gets said.
thread.weave: The member who finally reads his inventory to a sponsor often discovers that the thing he most wanted to leave out was the thing that most needed saying. A home group lives Tradition Five when a member gently steers a meeting back to alcoholism after it has wandered into politics or other problems, because the newcomer in the back came for one message and deserves to hear it. When a district or area assembly votes, Concept V asks the chair to invite the minority to speak, and more than once a minority voice has changed enough minds to reverse the outcome. At the Conference a delegate may bring a minority report, and any member with a personal grievance may petition for it to be carefully considered. Saying the exact nature of the thing, whether to a sponsor or to a roomful of delegates, is how A.A. keeps its integrity.
questions: What did I most want to leave out of my Fifth Step, and why did it need saying?
How does my home group keep its meetings focused on the one message it exists to carry?
When a vote goes against a minority in my group or district, do we ask to hear from them before moving on?

step.gist: Becoming fully ready to let go of our defects

tradition.gist: Staying clear of outside enterprises, endorsements and the money that follows

concept.gist: Trustees take the lead on most world service matters

thread.title: Willing to let go
thread.oneLiner: Willingness to be rid of what holds me back, what distracts the group, and what keeps the Conference from trusting its trustees.
thread.summary: Step Six is the willingness to be free of the defects we have come to depend on. Tradition Six asks the group to be just as willing to pass up money, property and prestige from outside ventures, however attractive, because they divert us from our purpose. Concept VI asks the Conference, which carries the principal responsibility for world services on the Fellowship's behalf, to be willing to let the trustees exercise chief initiative in most world service matters rather than micromanaging them. All three involve releasing something we are tempted to hold onto so that the real work can go forward.
thread.weave: A member working Step Six may notice that she is entirely ready to be rid of her temper but not her pride, and that the readiness has to grow one defect at a time. A home group faces Tradition Six when a well-meaning treatment center offers to print the group's schedule with its own logo, or a member wants to rent space for the group under a business name; the group says thank you and no. At the area level, committees decline to co-sponsor events with outside organizations, however worthy, so that nobody can mistake A.A. for an ally of anything but A.A. The Conference lives Concept VI every time it gives the General Service Board a broad advisory action and then trusts the trustees, A.A.W.S. and the Grapevine board to carry it out without a delegate committee second-guessing each step. Willingness, at every level, means loosening a grip.
questions: Which defect am I not yet entirely ready to lose, and what do I think it still does for me?
Has my group ever been offered something that would have tied A.A.'s name to an outside enterprise, and how did we decide?
How much initiative am I willing to let the trustees take before I want the Conference to step in?

step.gist: Asking, with humility, for help with our shortcomings

tradition.gist: Paying our own way, declining outside contributions

concept.gist: The board's legal power, balanced by the Conference's purse and tradition

thread.title: Who holds us up
thread.oneLiner: Humility asks God for help, self-support keeps the group free, and the groups' basket keeps the Conference and board in balance.
thread.summary: Step Seven asks us to approach God with humility, admitting we cannot fix ourselves and asking for help. Tradition Seven asks the group to pay its own way and decline outside money, so that no outside hand can steer it. Concept VII explains that the General Service Board holds legal authority under its charter, while the Conference's authority rests on tradition and on the power of the purse, the groups' own contributions. Humility, in all three, is knowing where our support truly comes from: from God for the individual, from ourselves for the group, and from the groups for the whole structure.
thread.weave: Humbly asking for help with a shortcoming, a member learns that the asking itself is the point, and that strength arrives from somewhere other than her own effort. A home group lives Tradition Seven when it declines a generous bequest from a grateful family, and when it takes a hard look at a prudent reserve that has grown larger than it needs and sends the rest along to its intergroup or central office, the district, the area and GSO. Those group contributions are the only money the Conference has to stand on, which is exactly what Concept VII means by the power of the purse: the trustees hold the legal title and the corporate powers, but the groups hold the checkbook and the trust. If the Fellowship ever stopped giving, the Conference would have no leverage, and if the board ever ignored the Conference, the groups would stop giving. Humility keeps the two in balance the way it keeps the individual leaning on God rather than on himself.
questions: What does humility feel like when I ask for help instead of trying harder?
Where does my group's Seventh Tradition money go after the basket is passed, and who decides?
If the groups' contributions are what give the Conference its authority, what does my group's giving say about our trust?

step.gist: Listing those we harmed and becoming willing to repair it

tradition.gist: Twelfth Step work is never paid for; service centers may employ special workers

concept.gist: Trustees plan broadly and oversee A.A.W.S. and the Grapevine

thread.title: Freely given, well stewarded
thread.oneLiner: Mending what we broke, helping one another for free, and trustees who steward without running everything: love that knows its job.
thread.summary: Step Eight turns our attention outward, toward the people we have harmed, and asks us to become willing to set things right out of something like love. Tradition Eight keeps our help for one another freely given, member to member, while allowing paid special workers for the practical jobs that keep the message moving. Concept VIII has the trustees act as planners and stewards of overall policy and finance, while leaving the day-to-day operation of A.A.W.S. and the Grapevine to their own directors. In each case, love for others shows up as a clear sense of what is ours to do, and what we must entrust to others.
thread.weave: Writing her Eighth Step list, a member stops arguing about who was more at fault and simply asks who she hurt, and that shift in attention is the beginning of brotherly love. In a home group, Tradition Eight is the member who answers the hotline at midnight for free, and it is also the group agreeing that the central office should hire a bookkeeper rather than burn out a volunteer. At GSO the staff members are A.A. members employed as special workers, working alongside nonalcoholic employees, all paid so that thousands of members can do Twelfth Step work unpaid. Concept VIII keeps the trustees from trying to edit every pamphlet or run the Grapevine's subscriptions themselves; they set policy, watch the finances and elect the directors of A.A.W.S. and the Grapevine, then let those boards do their jobs. Love, wherever it shows up, is caring enough to let the right people do the work.
questions: Whose name on my Eighth Step list am I still not willing to approach, and what would willingness look like?
Where in my group or central office does a paid special worker free members to carry the message?
What do the trustees actually do, and what do they leave to the A.A.W.S. and Grapevine boards?

step.gist: Going to those we harmed and setting things right

tradition.gist: No bosses or bureaucracy, just committees that answer to us

concept.gist: Good leaders, well chosen, at every level of service

thread.title: Directly responsible
thread.oneLiner: Direct amends, committees directly responsible to those they serve, and leaders who guide without governing: justice made visible.
thread.summary: Step Nine moves from willingness to action, going directly to those we harmed and doing what justice requires. Tradition Nine refuses to let A.A. become an organization of bosses, yet it creates service boards and committees that are directly responsible to the members they serve. Concept IX insists that good leaders, well chosen, are indispensable at every level, and that the trustees must take up the leadership once carried by Bill W. and Dr. Bob. Running through all three is a responsibility that is direct and personal: we face the people we owe, our committees face the groups they serve, and our leaders face the Fellowship rather than rule over it.
thread.weave: A member on Step Nine sits across a kitchen table from a sister he lied to for years and says plainly what he did, without excuses and without expecting forgiveness. Tradition Nine looks like a home group rotating its treasurer and secretary, keeping no permanent officers, and expecting each one to report back at the business meeting where anyone may ask questions. The district, the area committee, the delegate, the General Service Board and GSO are all Tradition Nine structures, and each stays responsible to the layer that created it; a DCM answers to GSRs, a delegate to the area, trustees to the Conference. Concept IX is about the quality of the people in those chairs: a good leader, in Bill W.'s description, originates ideas yet consults widely, listens, persuades, takes criticism, compromises where principle allows and stands firm where it does not. Justice in A.A. is not a courtroom; it is people showing up, face to face, to do what they said they would do.
questions: Which amends am I still making indirectly, by being nicer, when a direct one is called for?
Who does my group's committee or intergroup answer to, and how do members actually hold it responsible?
What qualities do I look for when I vote for a DCM, an area officer or a delegate?

step.gist: Keeping a daily inventory and promptly owning mistakes

tradition.gist: A.A. takes no sides on outside issues

concept.gist: Responsibility matched with equal, clearly defined authority

thread.title: Knowing where our job ends
thread.oneLiner: Daily inventory, no outside opinions, and every job with a clear scope: all three are about knowing where our business ends.
thread.summary: Step Ten asks us to keep watching our own conduct, every day, and to set things right as soon as we slip. Tradition Ten keeps A.A. as a whole watching its own conduct, declining to take public positions on outside issues so that we are never drawn into controversy. Concept X gives every service responsibility a matching authority and a well-defined scope, so that no trusted servant is answerable to two masters or tempted to reach beyond the job. The common thread is a disciplined sense of limits: knowing what is ours to tend, and tending only that.
thread.weave: Doing a Tenth Step at the end of the day, a member notices that she gave unsolicited advice at work again and makes a note to apologize, because perseverance is a daily habit, not a one-time cleanup. A home group practices Tradition Ten when a member wants to add a petition about a local ordinance to the literature table and the group kindly declines; the Washingtonians collapsed after taking on outside causes, and we have not forgotten. At the area level, Concept X shows up in a clear job description for the treasurer, with authority to pay routine bills without a vote on each one but also a defined limit beyond which the committee must decide. The trustees hold their legal authority under the board's charter and bylaws and their mandate from the Conference, GSO's general manager has authority from the A.A.W.S. board, and neither the delegates nor the trustees give orders to the staff, which is what Bill W. meant by avoiding double-headed management. Every level stays healthy by minding its own business and no one else's.
questions: What small slips do I tend to let slide until they become bigger problems?
How does my group handle a member who wants A.A. to take a public stand on something?
In my service position, what exactly am I authorized to decide, and to whom do I report?

step.gist: Growing closer to God through prayer and meditation

tradition.gist: Attraction, not promotion; staying anonymous in public media

concept.gist: Trustees surround themselves with skilled committees, directors, executives and staff

thread.title: The quiet work
thread.oneLiner: Prayer no one sees, recovery that speaks for itself, and skilled servants working out of the spotlight: depth, not display.
thread.summary: Step Eleven is a quiet, daily practice of prayer and meditation, improving our contact with God by listening more than talking. Tradition Eleven asks A.A. to let its results do the talking, attracting rather than promoting, with members keeping their personal anonymity before the press, radio, film and, today, online media. Concept XI asks the trustees to surround themselves with skilled committees, directors, executives and staff, and to care for them well, people whose competence and spirit do the Fellowship's work largely unseen. What they share is depth without display: the real power of A.A. is in what happens quietly, not in what gets attention.
thread.weave: A member who sits down each morning for a few minutes of prayer and meditation is building something no one else will ever see, and over time it shows in how she treats people. Tradition Eleven shows up when a district's public information committee places a simple notice in the paper that says where and when, with no member's face or last name, and trusts that a sober life is the best advertisement. At the area level the same spirit guides how officers are chosen: for steadiness and the ability to listen, not for charisma. At GSO, Concept XI is the staff member answering a Loner's letter, the Grapevine editor, the outside consultant or nonalcoholic friend who brings professional skill without seeking credit, and the rotation that keeps any one of them from becoming indispensable. Conscious contact, personal anonymity and competent service share one quality: they work best when nobody is watching.
questions: What does my daily practice of prayer and meditation actually look like, and what has it changed?
How does my group let A.A. speak for itself without promoting or putting faces forward?
Who serves on my area's committees and at GSO, and what do they do that I never see?

step.gist: Awakened, we carry the message and live the principles daily

tradition.gist: Anonymity keeps the focus on principles, not personalities

concept.gist: Six Warranties keep the Conference spiritual, prudent and democratic

thread.title: The spiritual foundation
thread.oneLiner: A spiritual awakening, anonymity as our foundation, and Warranties that keep the Conference spiritual: the ground under it all.
thread.summary: Step Twelve names the result of the first eleven, a spiritual awakening, and sends us out to carry the message and live by these principles everywhere. Tradition Twelve names the spiritual foundation beneath all the Traditions, anonymity, and the habit of placing principles ahead of personalities. Concept XII, through the six General Warranties, names the spiritual character the Conference must keep: wary of concentrated wealth or power; careful with money, keeping enough to operate plus an ample reserve; placing no member in unqualified authority over another; patient enough to seek substantial unanimity; never punishing anyone or stirring up public quarrels; and governing no one, staying democratic through and through. Each of the three Twelfths turns and looks back at the other eleven, saying that none of it works unless the foundation is spiritual.
thread.weave: The member who has had a spiritual awakening finds that it only stays alive if given away, so she picks up a newcomer for a meeting, chairs a step study and tries to practice patience at the dinner table. Her home group lives Tradition Twelve when a longtime member's strong personality loses a vote and he accepts it gracefully, because the principle mattered more than being right, and when nobody's sobriety date or profession buys extra weight at the business meeting. At the area assembly, the Warranties are in the room whenever a contentious motion passes by a bare majority and the body chooses to table it and talk more, aiming for substantial unanimity rather than a win. The Conference itself holds to the Warranties by keeping A.A.'s finances to enough to operate plus an ample reserve rather than a fortune, by refusing to punish any member or group, and by declining to perform acts of government over anyone. Service, spirituality and the Warranties are three names for the same foundation, which is why the tapestry holds together.
questions: How do I carry the message in ways that have nothing to do with speaking at a meeting?
When has my group put a principle ahead of a personality, including my own?
Which of the six Warranties does my district, area or group most need to remember right now?
